idiom_name: registered listener/callback + container-owned delivery loop (asynchronous receiver)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define a narrow listener interface (one handler method that receives the message plus a callback context for ack/nack), register it with the transport's consumer API, and let the container or client own the receive loop, the threading model and the session lifecycle; the application never calls receive(). Keep the endpoint object free of connection management, and make the delivery policy (concurrency, prefetch, ack mode, redelivery, dead-letter) explicit configuration of the container rather than code inside the handler. Where no container exists, hand-write the smallest equivalent - a dispatcher thread, event loop or runtime that performs the blocking receive and invokes the listener - plus reconnection and a shutdown drain.
code_sketch:
listener = MessageListener { on_message(msg, ctx) { handle(msg); ctx.ack() } }
consumer = transport.create_consumer(queue, prefetch=1, ack_mode="manual")
consumer.set_listener(listener)      # the messaging system invokes us
consumer.start()                     # container owns the receive loop
                                     # application thread: idle, no receive() call
pitfalls: Calling receive() or a sleep/retry loop inside the handler reintroduces the polling consumer under an event-driven facade.
Assuming the container is single-threaded; concurrency is configuration (prefetch, concurrent consumers, dispatcher threads).
Acknowledging before the work is durably done loses messages on crash - auto-ack is not transactional.
Not draining in-flight messages on shutdown duplicates work and can lose acknowledgements.

Wrong move: doing slow work directly on the client's callback thread (Paho's on_message runs on the network loop thread) -> keepalive pings go unanswered and the broker drops the connection -> instead hand the message to a worker queue so the callback returns promptly.

Wrong move: relying on auto-ack where the transport acknowledges at receipt (Paho acks after on_message returns; JMS AutoAcknowledged after the listener returns) -> a crash mid-handler loses the message with no redelivery -> instead switch to manual ack and acknowledge only after the effect is durable.

Wrong move: buffering pushed messages in an unbounded in-memory queue so the callback can return fast -> a write burst grows the buffer until the heap is exhausted because push ignores downstream capacity (Camel's unbounded realtime change buffer, CAMEL-24525) -> instead bound the buffer, cap concurrent handlers and let prefetch or pause push back-pressure to the broker.
